title: Walk Off Deimos: 14 km
body:
A recent analysis by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory has revealed that a spacecraft could skim the surface of Mars’s tiny moon Deimos at a speed barely faster than a brisk walk—about 14 kilometres per hour (km/h). Push that pace up to roughly 20 km/h and the vehicle would achieve escape velocity, shedding the moon’s weak gravitational grip entirely. The figures, derived from JPL’s precise measurements of Deimos’s mass and dimensions, underscore how dramatically orbital dynamics change on small bodies compared with Earth, where orbital speeds soar into the tens of thousands of kilometres per hour.

Deimos, the smaller of Mars’s two moons, measures just 15 km across and weighs a mere 1.8 × 10¹⁵ kg. Its surface gravity is approximately 0.003 m/s²—about 0.03 % of Earth’s. In such a feeble field, the velocity needed to maintain a low‑altitude orbit (effectively “grazing” the surface) is calculated to be 14.2 km/h, a speed comparable to an elite racewalker’s stride. By contrast, a modest increase to 20.1 km/h would give a spacecraft enough kinetic energy to break free from Deimos’s pull, sending it into a Mars‑centric trajectory or deeper into interplanetary space.

The numbers may seem almost whimsical, but they have practical implications for future exploration missions. A lander or hopper designed to bounce across Deimos could, in theory, use tiny thrusters to accelerate just a few metres per second and transition from a surface‑hugging orbit to a free‑flight escape. This would dramatically reduce fuel requirements compared with missions to larger bodies, where orbital insertion and departure demand massive propulsion systems. Engineers could therefore contemplate lightweight, low‑cost probes that “walk” around Deimos, mapping its regolith, sampling its composition, and even testing technologies for asteroid mining or planetary defense.

However, the simplicity of the calculations belies the complexities introduced by the irregular shapes of both Deimos and its parent planet, Mars. Deimos’s ellipsoidal form and its slightly eccentric orbit mean that the local gravity vector varies across the surface, and tidal forces from Mars introduce subtle perturbations. Moreover, the moon’s proximity to Mars—about 23 000 km above the Martian atmosphere—exposes any nearby spacecraft to the planet’s tenuous exosphere and magnetic environment, which could affect navigation and communications. Mission planners will need to model these factors in three dimensions, using high‑resolution shape models and real‑time tracking data to ensure safe operations.

The contrast with Earth is stark. To achieve low Earth orbit, a vehicle must travel at roughly 28 000 km/h, and a projectile would need a launch speed near 40 000 km/h to escape Earth’s gravity altogether. Even the International Space Station, a massive laboratory orbiting at 7.66 km/s, dwarfs the modest velocities required around Deimos. This disparity highlights why small bodies present unique opportunities for low‑energy missions, but also why they demand careful consideration of non‑Keplerian effects such as solar radiation pressure, which can become a dominant force when gravitational attraction is so weak.

Looking ahead, the newfound understanding of Deimos’s orbital mechanics could shape the design of upcoming missions to the Martian system. NASA’s upcoming “Moon‑Deimos” concept—a small, reusable hopper intended to ferry scientific payloads between the two moons—relies on precisely these low‑speed dynamics. As agencies and private firms eye the moons of Mars as stepping stones for deeper exploration, the ability to “walk” around Deimos at walking speed may become a cornerstone of cost‑effective, high‑frequency reconnaissance, paving the way for more ambitious endeavors across the Solar System.
